title: Matthew 15:21–28
context: Jesus withdraws into the region of Tyre and Sidon. A Canaanite woman cries for mercy to the Son of David for her demon-oppressed daughter. After silence, a word about Israel’s lost sheep, and a hard saying about children’s bread, her faith answers with crumbs from the masters’ table. Jesus praises her great faith; her daughter is healed instantly.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: On faith, mercy, and the nations, a few classic voices from each tradition.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Saving faith… is a divine evidence and conviction, not only that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, but also that Christ loved me, and gave himself for me. It is by this faith… that we receive Christ.

I ascribe to grace the commencement, the continuance and the consummation of all good… The controversy… relates solely to the mode of operation, whether it be irresistible or not… I believe, according to the scriptures, that many persons resist the Holy Spirit and reject the grace that is offered.

reformed.quote: This woman is a mother… She does not cease to pray… Faith is not always equally vigorous; but… when it is tried, it shines more brightly.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 15:22–28)

reformed.quote: Faith is the gift of God… We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God.
reformed.source: “Faith: What Is It? How Can It Be Obtained?” (echoing Eph 2:8; 2 Cor 3:5)

verses.text: Jesus went out from there and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus withdraws northwest toward Tyre and Sidon. Gentile coasts become the next stage after conflict with Jerusalem’s teachers.

The Lord places Himself where outsiders can find Him. Grace crosses borders; hearers in every district remain summoned to seek mercy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Withdrawal is purposeful geography. The Son moves into a Gentile district under the Father’s plan, not as aimless retreat.

Tyre and Sidon will host a revelation of faith that shames much of Israel’s privilege. Providence orders the map of mercy.

verses.text: Behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those borders and cried, saying, “Have mercy on me, Lord, you son of David! My daughter is severely possessed by a demon!”
verses.arminianNotes:
A Canaanite woman comes crying: mercy, Lord, Son of David. She uses Israel’s royal title for a daughter’s demonic oppression.

Here the reader meets remarkable light. Grace has taught her who Jesus is; she responds with persistent petition. Maternal love and true faith meet in one cry.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew’s “behold” flags wonder: a Canaanite names Jesus Lord and Son of David. Faith speaks Israel’s confession from outside Israel’s house.

Such confession is gift. The Spirit opens Gentile lips to the Messiah before the bread of the children is formally extended.

verses.text: But he answered her not a word. His disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away; for she cries after us.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus’ silence is authentic and hard. The disciples want dismissal; her crying annoys their journey.

Silence is not absence of compassion. Faith that keeps asking under quiet skies is still meeting a gracious Lord who will speak.
verses.reformedNotes:
At first Jesus gives her no word at all. Disciples prefer an exit over engagement. Christ’s delay serves a larger unveiling of faith.

The Lord’s timing includes silence that deepens petition. What looks like neglect is often the forge of greater trust.

verses.text: But he answered, “I wasn’t sent to anyone but the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus names His mission priority: the lost sheep of Israel. The gospel’s order is not racism; it is covenantal sequence that still leaves room for Gentile mercy.

Israel first, and a sincere wideness that will bless the nations. This woman is not lied to; she is placed inside a redemptive order that grace is already stretching.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Son states His sentness: Israel’s lost sheep. Messianic mission has an appointed first audience.

Christ’s words are true, not a bluff. Yet within that priority the Father has prepared a Gentile faith that will receive crumbs as feast—and later the nations in fullness.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm Israel’s priority in Jesus’ earthly mission and coming mercy for Gentiles. Arminians stress a sincere, grace-enabled invitation that this woman rightly presses into; Reformed readers press the Messiah’s ordered mission and the Father’s sovereign gift of faith that pierces that order without denying it.

verses.text: But she came and worshiped him, saying, “Lord, help me.”
verses.arminianNotes:
She advances, kneels, and shortens the prayer: “Lord, help me.” Persistence becomes worship.

Faith does not quit when the first answers are hard. Grace sustains kneeling; the will truly seeks help from Jesus alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Nearer and lower: she kneels. The plea is pure dependence—“help me.”

True faith is humble and Christward. The Lord who seemed distant is the only helper she names.

verses.text: But he answered, “It is not appropriate to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The saying is severe: children’s bread is not for dogs. Household order is pictured; Gentiles stand outside as “dogs” in the proverb’s starkness.

Arminians do not soften the hardness, yet hear a test that faith may answer. Grace enables her to receive the word without rage and to find an opening inside it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jesus speaks the barrier in household language. Israel’s children have first claim on the bread of the kingdom.

The distinction is true in redemptive history. The wonder is not that He said it, but that faith will bow under it and still cling to Him.
verses.keyContrast: Both refuse to pretend the saying was soft. Arminians detect a severe test that grace enables her to answer without despair; Reformed Christians hear truthful mission order under which God will magnify a faith He Himself sustains.

verses.text: But she said, “Yes, Lord, but even the dogs eat the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Yes, Lord”—she accepts the premise, then finds mercy in the crumbs. Humility and wit meet trust: even dogs eat under the masters’ table.

She does not demand the children’s portion; she pleads for overflow. Grace-taught faith agrees with Jesus and still expects kindness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Her “yes” submits; her yet believes. Crumbs from the masters’ table are enough if they come from this Master.

Faith argues from Jesus’ own metaphor toward hope. The logic is given by God; the answer will prove crumbs to be a feast of power.
verses.keyContrast: Both praise her humble, ingenious trust. Arminians stress a free, grace-enabled response that agrees with Christ and seeks mercy; Reformed commentators stress faith as God’s gift arguing rightly from Christ’s word toward certain help.

verses.text: Then Jesus answered her, “Woman, great is your faith! Be it done to you even as you desire.” And her daughter was healed from that hour.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus praises “great” faith and grants her desire; the daughter is healed instantly. Faith is honored as trust that receives.

The Lord’s commendation takes her faith seriously as a living response under grace. Gentile seekers are truly welcomed when they cling to the Son of David.
verses.reformedNotes:
Christ names her faith great and effectually heals. Desire aligned with trust meets the Son’s sovereign “Be it done.”

Great faith is recognized because God wrought it; instant healing displays the King’s authority beyond Israel’s borders already.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess great faith and instant mercy. Arminians stress faith as grace-enabled trust that truly receives Christ’s gift; Reformed interpreters typically emphasize that such great faith and the healing are God’s effectual work through the Son who wills the daughter well.
